cases.title: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words
cases.request: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words: how an LLM judge decides a delivery.
cases.delivery:
Imagine you're at a post office, and you need to send a package to a friend. You give the post office your friend's address, and they tell you that it's going to take a few days to arrive. But then, you ask the post office how long it will take to arrive, and they say it will be 3-5 days. You're not sure if you trust their answer, because it's not like you know the exact route the package will take.

A Large Language Model (LLM) is kind of like that post office. It's a computer program that can understand and generate human-like text. But instead of sending packages, an LLM is used to judge things. In this case, the LLM is judging a delivery based on the information it has.

The LLM looks at all the data it has, like the address you gave it, and the information it has about the route the package will take. It then uses that information to make a decision about how long the package will arrive. But the LLM doesn't just rely on the data

cases.title: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words
cases.request: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words: why a hire on Cadre is held in escrow.
cases.delivery:
When you hire someone on a Cadre, it's not just about finding a skilled individual to work with. It's also about protecting both parties. A hire on Cadre is typically held in escrow, which means that the employer and the hired person agree to a temporary delay in payment until certain conditions are met.

This is usually the case when the hired person is working on a high-stakes project, or when the employer needs time to finalize a contract or negotiate with other parties. By holding the payment in escrow, both sides can avoid any potential disputes or misunderstandings.

The escrow process helps to prevent misunderstandings and ensures that both parties are committed to the agreement. It's a way of saying, "We're in this together, and we need to make sure we're both on the same page."

cases.title: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words
cases.request: Plain-words explainer, about 120 words: what a paid thought receipt proves and what it does not.
cases.delivery:
A paid thought receipt is a document that proves you've paid for something, like a service or a product. It's usually created by the person or business you've paid for, and it shows the amount you've paid and the date you paid. This receipt is like a receipt for your receipt, showing that you've actually paid for what you bought.

The paid thought receipt is important because it helps you keep track of your expenses and makes it easier to get your money back if something goes wrong. It's also useful if you need to prove that you paid for something, like if you're disputing a charge on your credit card or if you need to claim a refund.
